title_original: Jordan Rossi: “Joy Is Political in Its Own Way”
excerpt_original: In "Homecoming", presented during Milan Fashion Week, the British photographer and filmmaker probes identity, masculinity and queer culture at the intersection of fashion photography, fine art portraiture and social reflection. L’article Jordan Rossi: “Joy Is Political in Its…

blocks.text: Jordan Rossi has always walked a fine line. British with Italian and Irish roots, he shoots the London queer scene and luxury brand campaigns with equal conviction, never appearing to betray either. His gaze turns fashion photography — vivid, often irreverent — into a tool for intimate and social portraiture. With a single obsession: catching the moment his subjects drop the mask.
The title of your first exhibition, “Homecoming”, speaks of both return and belonging. What does that word mean to you?

Jordan Rossi : “Homecoming” felt like the only possible title. I grew up between two cultures, Italian and Irish, but I was born and raised in London — so I’ve always had a slightly complicated relationship with the idea of “home”. I don’t think I’ve ever felt entirely one thing or another.

Bringing this body of work to Italy feels like closing a circle. These photographs cover nearly a decade of my life, made in London, Los Angeles and elsewhere. Bringing them here, to a country that is part of my identity and my family, feels very personal. But with time, “home” has become less geographical for me. It’s the people you surround yourself with, the communities you find, and eventually the space you create for yourself. In that sense, “Homecoming” is as much about where I am now as it is about where I came from.

blocks.caption: Lukita Maxwell © Jordan Rossi, courtesy of the artist and Galleria Rubin

blocks.text: You have shot the queer community of East London just as much as campaigns for Rolls-Royce. Are these two worlds not in conflict, and how do you move between them?

Jordan Rossi : I’ve never really seen them as being in conflict. The scale, budgets and expectations might be completely different, but ultimately I’m still interested in the same things: people, character, and creating a world around them.

I also don’t think queer artists should have to exist solely within queer spaces. I can photograph someone in a club in East London and then direct a campaign for a global brand — both can still contain my point of view. If anything, moving between those worlds matters to me. The experiences and communities that shaped me inevitably find their way into the commercial work, and the resources of the commercial world feed back into my personal work. I don’t want either side of my career to exist in isolation from the other.
Your photography is generally described as queer, committed, rooted in fashion and portraiture. What would you add about your work and where it has taken you?

Jordan Rossi : I’d probably add that there’s a sense of performance running through a lot of it. I’m interested in the version of ourselves that we construct for the camera: fashion, sexuality, masculinity, femininity, celebrity, glamour. Portraiture can document somebody, but it can also give them permission to become something else for a moment.

Over the past decade that has taken me into very different rooms — from emerging performers and people within the queer community to actors, musicians, fashion houses and global brands. I’ve photographed people I admired long before I ever picked up a camera professionally, which still feels slightly surreal. But when I look across the work now, what interests me isn’t necessarily who is famous and who isn’t. It’s that the same curiosity runs through all of it. I’m drawn to people who have a strong sense of who they are — or who are in the process of discovering it.

blocks.text: You are a photographer, a filmmaker and a creative director all at once. Concretely, how do you hold those three roles together?
Jordan Rossi : What I’ve realised over time is that every time I’ve added another discipline, it has changed the way I approach everything else.

There are instincts and skills that move between them. Photography made me much more aware of the relationship you build with the person in front of your camera. It can be incredibly intimate — just two people trying to find something together. Learning how to create that trust changed the way I worked with performers when I returned to directing. In the same way, years of filmmaking and creative direction have made me think differently about still images. I’m rarely just thinking about whether something looks beautiful; I’m thinking about the world around it, the character, the emotion, and what the image is trying to say.

That’s ultimately how I hold all three together: they’ve become part of the same visual language. I’m constantly taking things I’ve learned in one area into another, often without consciously realizing it. I’m less interested now in whether something makes me a photographer, director or creative director — and more interested in finding the best way to tell the story in front of me.
In your work, you have chosen to show the joy of the LGBTQIA+ community rather than its trauma. Do you feel a particular responsibility towards that community — and if so, what does it look like?
Jordan Rossi : Absolutely — although I try not to let that responsibility turn into the idea that there is one correct way to represent a community as enormous and varied as ours.

For a long time, so many LGBTQIA+ stories were framed through tragedy, rejection or suffering. Those stories are real and important, but they aren’t the entirety of queer life. I became much more interested in photographing the other side of it: friendship, sex, humor, beauty, ridiculousness, confidence, intimacy and joy. Not as a denial of the difficult things, but because those things are also political in their own way. There is power in seeing queer people simply having a brilliant time, taking up space, being desired rather than apologising for being there.

My responsibility is really to the people in front of my camera. I want them to feel they have agency in how they’re represented, and I want the work to come from being part of a community rather than looking at it from the outside. I don’t think my job is to speak for LGBTQIA+ people. It’s to contribute my perspective to a much bigger, messier and more interesting story.
